metric_rationale: We isolate the trials where Cue-Parity and Tallying make strictly opposite predictions. On trials where A wins on 2 or 4 cues and B wins on 0 or 1 (mask_123), Cue-Parity predicts B (because 2 and 4 are even) while Tallying predicts A (because A has more wins). Conversely, on trials where A wins on 1 cue and B wins on 2 or 3 (mask_45), Cue-Parity predicts A (because 1 is odd) while Tallying predicts B. By taking the difference in the proportion of B choices between these two sets of trials, we get a metric that is approximately +1 for Cue-Parity and -1 for Tallying, providing maximal discriminability.

This metric calculates the proportion of responses that align with Cue-Parity's deterministic predictions specifically on trials where the tally is tied (i.e., option A and option B win on an equal number of features). On these trials, Tallying predicts complete indifference (50% chance for A or B), yielding an expected metric value of 0.5. Cue-Parity, however, makes deterministic choices based on the parity of the wins (predicting A if odd, B if even), yielding an expected metric value close to 1.0 (subject only to the epsilon lapse rate).

This metric computes the exact agreement proportion between the subject's choices and the 5-feature Cue-Parity rule. The advocated theory (Cue-Parity) will score near 1.0 (subject to noise) because it uses all 5 features to compute parity. The competing theory (Lexicographic Parity) typically uses only the top 3 or 4 cues (due to k_frac in [0.5, 1.0]), which reverses the parity prediction on 6 out of 8 trials. Thus, the competing theory will yield an average agreement around 0.4, providing a massive, highly significant contrast.

This metric isolates trials where the parity of A-wins on the top 3 most valid cues differs strictly from the parity of A-wins across all 6 cues. On these trials, Cue-Parity will systematically predict the opposite of the top-3 parity rule, resulting in a score near 0. Lexicographic Parity, depending on the exact value of k_frac, will sometimes rely exactly on the top 3 cues, yielding a higher expected match rate. The strong divergence in predictions on this subset of trials guarantees robust discrimination between the two models.

Under Cue-Parity, choices are determined strictly by whether the unweighted sum of A-wins is odd or even. Thus, the probability of choosing A should be identical for sum=7 and sum=5 (both odd), and the probability of choosing B should be identical for sum=4 and sum=6 (both even), yielding a metric value near 0. Under Continuous Weighted Parity, validities perturb the sums. Sums of 5 and 6 are pushed towards half-integers (the 'dead zones' of the cosine parity function), which heavily degrades their choice probability. Sums of 4 and 7 remain closer to integers, retaining strong choice probabilities. This causes the metric to be strongly positive for Continuous Weighted Parity.

This metric leverages a mathematically perfect invariant of Cue-Parity to achieve zero expected bias and extremely low variance. For Cue-Parity, T1/T2 (5 wins) are odd, so it predicts A with probability P. T3/T4 (4 wins) are even, so it predicts B with the exact same probability P, meaning it chooses A with probability 1-P. The sum of the log-odds of choosing A for these two groups is strictly log(P/(1-P)) + log((1-P)/P) = 0, regardless of the subject's temperature or lapse rate. However, for Continuous Weighted Parity, the validity weights shift the sum. For T1/T2, the score is cos(1.25*pi*w), which is severely attenuated or even negative. For T3/T4, the score is -cos(pi*w), which is also attenuated but structurally less so than T1/T2. Because cos(1.25*pi*w) < cos(pi*w) for all w > 0, the push towards A on T1/T2 is strictly weaker than the push towards B on T3/T4. Thus, the sum of log-odds is systematically negative for CWP. By returning the negative sum, we get a metric that is robustly positive for CWP and exactly zero for Cue-Parity.

By comparing trials where Cue-Parity makes identical predictions but the validity-weighted tally strongly shifts from favoring Option A to Option B, we can isolate the effect of the tallying fallback mechanism. Cue-Parity predicts identical probabilities (difference around 0), while Tallying-Biased Parity predicts a systematic positive shift in the choice probabilities across these paired trials.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing option A between pairs of trials that have the exact same Cue-Parity status but opposite Tallying (validity-weighted) status. Pure Cue-Parity predicts these differences will be exactly zero on average, as it ignores validities. Tallying-Biased Parity predicts a strictly positive value because the fallback tallying strategy will systematically increase the probability of choosing A when the high-validity cues favor A compared to when they favor B.

By comparing the Cue-Parity match rate on trials where option A wins on the lowest-validity cue (trials 2, 4, 6, 8) versus trials where it loses (trials 1, 3, 5, 7), we can perfectly separate the two models. Cue-Parity will have a high match rate on both sets, yielding a difference near 0. Top-K Parity, which drops the lowest-validity cue half the time (when k=19), will systematically reverse its prediction on the target trials while maintaining the same prediction on control trials, yielding a strongly negative difference.

In an 11-feature task with k_frac ~ U(0.9, 1.0), Top-K Parity will evaluate exactly 10 cues for ~9% of subjects (when k_frac <= 0.909) and 11 cues for the rest. Cue-Parity always evaluates 11 cues. On trials where the 11th cue differs between options, 10-cue parity and 11-cue parity make strictly opposite predictions. By computing the match rate to the 10-cue parity prediction, Cue-Parity subjects will score near 0 (modulo epsilon noise), while the ~9% of Top-K Parity subjects using k=10 will score near 1. Returning the maximum subject score from the pooled dataset forces a massive difference in the point estimate (~1.0 for Top-K vs ~0.3 for Cue-Parity) while preserving tight subject-level variances, satisfying the t-test at N=25.
